question: Tell me about a process you removed because it bought consistency and nothing else.

raiseTranscript.text: On my team we had a weekly status email that everyone copied to a shared folder. I noticed no one read the archives and it took 30 minutes each week. I proposed dropping it and switching to a 5-minute standup note instead. My manager agreed after I showed the last three months had zero lookups.
What was the follow-up? How did you measure impact?
I tracked open rates on the new notes for a month and asked the team if anything was missed. Zero issues, so we kept it gone.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a process you removed because it bought consistency and nothing else.
Candidate identified weekly status email archive that no one used.
Measured by checking folder access logs over 3 months (zero reads).
Replaced with lighter standup note after manager sign-off.
Quote: "Zero lookups in the last three months."
Follow-up: Tracked new note engagement for a month and confirmed no gaps.
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Efficiency. The candidate owned removal of an unused weekly archive process at the individual level. They checked access logs for three months showing zero reads before proposing the change and validated the replacement for a month. Quote: "Zero lookups in the last three months." This shows basic bias for action and measurement within their own workflow. The main gap is lack of any cross-team coordination or longer-term tracking beyond one month.

Not really, I just assumed it was needed for consistency.

This reflects passive acceptance of process rather than any attempt to measure or remove waste, even at the individual level.

raiseTranscript.text: Across three teams we had a monthly compliance checklist that duplicated our existing CI checks. I pulled usage data showing 95% auto-pass rate and ran a two-week pilot removing it for one team. After no incidents we rolled it out and saved roughly 40 hours per month.
How did you get buy-in from the other teams?
I shared the pilot metrics in a shared doc and let each team lead decide. Two adopted immediately, the third after seeing the first month of results.

raiseTranscript.text: At the org level we had a quarterly planning ritual that required every team to produce 20-slide decks even though leadership only used the top three metrics. I ran an analysis showing 1200 hours spent annually and replaced it with a 2-page template plus optional deep-dive sessions. Adoption reached 85% within two quarters and planning cycle time dropped 30%.
What trade-offs did you consider with the teams that resisted?
We kept an opt-in deep-dive track for complex programs and tracked whether any missed items surfaced in the first two cycles. None did.
